Mixture-of-experts (MoE) transformers route each token to a small subset of specialized feed-forward "expert" networks via a learned gating function, achieving high parameter counts without proportional compute costs. The central question here is: when the input distribution shifts at inference time (domain change, covariate shift, adversarial prompts), does the router continue to distribute tokens meaningfully across experts, or does it collapse — sending a disproportionate share of tokens to a few experts while others go idle? The key concepts are load balancing (enforced during training via auxiliary losses), router confidence calibration, and the distinction between token-choice routing (each token picks its top-k experts) versus expert-choice routing (each expert picks its top-k tokens), which have asymmetric failure modes under shift. What a beginner misses is that the auxiliary balancing loss is computed over the training distribution, so a router that appears perfectly balanced on the training set can catastrophically over-concentrate under even modest distribution shift — not because experts become less capable, but because the router's learned soft boundaries are brittle decision surfaces in a high-dimensional space that the shift crosses. The expert's deeper worry is that this collapse is largely invisible in aggregate metrics: perplexity or task accuracy may degrade only modestly while the model has effectively become a dense network using 10% of its parameters, wasting capacity and potentially generating confidently wrong outputs in the collapsed experts' domains.
